newsitem.title: KENYA: Drought cuts Kenyan growth prospects.
newsitem.headline: Drought cuts Kenyan growth prospects.

text.p: Drought which lasted into the first quarter of 1997 has severely undermined Kenya's manufacturing and agriculture sectors and will cut economic growth by more than initially forecast, business chiefs said on Tuesday.
They predicted interest rates would remain high in the financial year ending June 1998 and inflation would rise beyond the central bank's single-digit target.
Failed rains from October 1996 to March 1997 will mean a drop in output figures for top commodities such as tea, coffee and horticultural products, they said without giving specific details.
"The picture painted of the next year is very bleak," said Levi Wendo, Kenya's Commissioner of Income Tax, addressing a gathering of business executives in the capital Nairobi.

Chris Key, commercial director at leading agricultural concern Brooke Bond, said that gross domestic product growth would be around 2.0 percent in 1997 compared to Finance Minister Musalia Mudavadi's forecast of 4.0 percent.
"Growth rates will be much lower than last year. Prices (of goods) are too high, manufacturing is not expanding. Drought also may have a more serious effect than stated," said Key.
"I don't see where growth will come from," Key added.

Mudavadi sees GDP growth down to 4.0 percent from 4.6 percent in 1996 and 4.8 percent in 1995. Mudavadi said drought forced annual inflation up to 12.3 percent in the first quarter of 1997 against government projections of single-digit inflation.
Key said inflation was likely to be about 15 percent.
Benchmark interest rates on 91-day treasury bills stand at around 19.2 percent. Central Bank Governor Micah Cheserem on Monday told Reuters that they would continue to ease in 1997.

Charles Gardner, resident representative of the East Africa Association that groups British companies in Kenya, said poor infrastructure and corruption were also viewed by investors as undermining all efforts at increased economic growth.
Gardner said his group had given these views to government.

"On issues such as corruption, we believe the only method that will work is prosecuting and convicting those who bribe and those who are bribed. Taking steps that make it difficult to bribe is not the answer, people always have a way," he said.
Gardner said it was disturbing that many people got away with serious crimes in Kenya which was bad news for investors.

He cited the unresolved murders of British tourist Julie Ward and Kenyan Foreign Minister Robert Ouko, and the so-called Goldenberg Scandal, in which the Treasury paid millions of dollars in compensation for gold exports that did not exist.

"You would expect the Attorney-General and Commissioner of Police to resign for not resolving these crimes. If they prosecuted the wrong people, you would expect them to resign over that as well. That has not happened here," Gardner said.

John Munge, executive director at leading brokerage company Shah, Munge & Partners, said it was important to continue the process of democratisation and encourage a dissident voice "in order to emphasis checks and balances necessary for growth".
Munge said more tolerance was needed in government in order to continue the necessary economic reforms for faster growth.
In his 1997/98 state budget, Mudavadi made infrastructure key to his plans. He spoke of reform in the power sector, as well as telecommunications, roads and railways.
He also spoke of launching a Eurobond as an alternative method of government borrowing to reduce domestic debt.
($1= 55 shillings).
